# Tracking Changes

## The rhythm of Git

Every version you save follows the same two-step rhythm:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

- Edit your files as usual
- [`git add`]{.uwred} — mark the changes you want to save
- [`git commit`]{.uwred} — save them as a point in history

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Along the way, three commands let you check in:

- [`git status`]{.uwred} — where do things stand?
- [`git diff`]{.uwred} — what exactly changed?
- [`git log`]{.uwred} — what have I saved so far?


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Put the first item on the menu

Bucky starts with the main event. Open a new file with `nano`:

```bash
nano brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Type one line, then save and exit with [Ctrl+X]{.uwred}, then [Y]{.uwred}, then [Enter]{.uwred}:

```
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Prefer a different editor? Open the file in the RStudio [source editor]{.uwred}, or use another terminal editor like [vim]{.uwred} (my preferred editor) — any of them works. These slides use `nano`. Either way, nothing has been handed to Git yet; we have only written to the folder.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A new, untracked file

Check in with `git status`:

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	brats.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Git sees `brats.txt` but calls it [untracked]{.uwred} — it is not yet part of the history.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 1 of 2: stage it with `git add`

Tell Git this file belongs in the next saved version:

```bash
git add brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

This puts `brats.txt` on the [stage]{.uwred} — the group of changes that will be saved together on your next commit.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

`git add` produces no output when it succeeds. Run `git status` to see what it did.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Staged and ready

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Now Git lists `brats.txt` under [Changes to be committed]{.uwred}. It is staged, but not yet saved to history.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2 of 2: save it with `git commit`

A [commit]{.uwred} is a permanent point in your history. It needs a short message describing the change:

```bash
git commit -m "Add brats to the menu"
```

```
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add brats to the menu
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The `-m` flag supplies the message. This is our first commit, so Git labels it the [root-commit]{.uwred} and stamps it with a unique ID (a1b2c3d).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Working tree clean

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

[Working tree clean]{.uwred} means the folder matches the saved history exactly — nothing is waiting to be saved.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where your work lives

That two-step dance makes sense once you see the three places your work can be:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
  <th>Working directory</th>
  <th>Staging area</th>
  <th>Repository</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td>Your files as you edit them</td>
  <td>Changes you have marked to save</td>
  <td>The permanent history of commits</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Two commands move your work to the right along this path.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## `git add` moves work to the stage

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
  <th class="hl">Working directory</th>
  <th class="hl">Staging area</th>
  <th>Repository</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td class="hl">Your files as you edit them</td>
  <td class="hl">Changes you have marked to save</td>
  <td>The permanent history of commits</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="gap-md"></div>

[`git add`]{.uwred} copies changes from your working directory onto the stage. You choose exactly what goes on.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## `git commit` records the stage

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
  <th>Working directory</th>
  <th class="hl">Staging area</th>
  <th class="hl">Repository</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td>Your files as you edit them</td>
  <td class="hl">Changes you have marked to save</td>
  <td class="hl">The permanent history of commits</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="gap-md"></div>

[`git commit`]{.uwred} records everything on the stage as one point in history. The extra step is a feature: it lets you group related changes into a single, meaningful commit.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## See your history: `git log`

```bash
git log
```

```
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Bucky Badger <bucky@wisc.edu>
Date:   Fri Oct 9 10:15:00 2026 -0500

    Add brats to the menu
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Each commit records the full ID, who made it, when, and the message. [HEAD]{.uwred} marks where you are now.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bucky tweaks the brats

How many to buy? Reopen the file:

```bash
nano brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Add a second line, then save and exit:

```
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Save the file, then check what Git thinks.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A tracked file, now modified

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   brats.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

This time Git already knows `brats.txt`, so it reports it as [modified]{.uwred} rather than untracked.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What exactly changed? `git diff`

Came back from the stadium and forgot what you edited? Ask Git:

```bash
git diff brats.txt
```

<pre><code><strong>diff --git a/brats.txt b/brats.txt
index 83db48f..f735c2d 100644
--- a/brats.txt
+++ b/brats.txt</strong>
<span style="color:teal;">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
<span style="color:forestgreen;">+Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)</span>
</code></pre>

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Git colors the output: added lines show in <span style="color:forestgreen;">green</span> with a `+`, and removed lines would show in <span style="color:red;">red</span> with a `-`.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Stage and commit the edit

Same two steps as before:

```bash
git add brats.txt
git commit -m "Note how many brats to buy"
```

```
[main b2c3d4e] Note how many brats to buy
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

That is the whole rhythm: [edit → add → commit]{.uwred}. You will do it hundreds of times.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## One commit, two new files

The menu grows. Create two more files, one at a time:

```bash
nano cheese_curds.txt
```

```
Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets
```

```bash
nano desserts.txt
```

```
Babcock ice cream - chocolate and Union Blend
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```bash
git status
```

```
Untracked files:
	cheese_curds.txt
	desserts.txt
```


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Stage both at once

These two go together, so stage them in one step:

```bash
git add cheese_curds.txt desserts.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Preview what is staged with `git diff --staged` (plain `git diff` looks only at unstaged changes):

```bash
git diff --staged
```

<pre><code><strong>diff --git a/cheese_curds.txt b/cheese_curds.txt
new file mode 100644</strong>
<span style="color:teal;">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span style="color:forestgreen;">+Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets</span>
<strong>diff --git a/desserts.txt b/desserts.txt
new file mode 100644</strong>
<span style="color:teal;">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span style="color:forestgreen;">+Babcock ice cream - chocolate and Union Blend</span>
</code></pre>


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Commit them together

Both new files land in [one]{.uwred} commit:

```bash
git commit -m "Add cheese curds and desserts"
```

```
[main c3d4e5f] Add cheese curds and desserts
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 cheese_curds.txt
 create mode 100644 desserts.txt
```

<div class="gap-md"></div>

This is why `add` and `commit` are separate steps: you decide what belongs together.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Later, we will learn how to undo a commit so best to stage and commit edits that represent some block of changes that belong together for some goal in your development/analysis workflow


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The story so far: `git log --oneline`

Full `git log` gets long fast. The `--oneline` flag gives one row per commit:

```bash
git log --oneline
```

```
c3d4e5f (HEAD -> main) Add cheese curds and desserts
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

You can also limit the count: `git log -2` shows just the two most recent commits.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Name a file to see only the commits that changed it — handy when you need to track down an error in one file:

```bash
git log --oneline brats.txt
```

```
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The cheese curds and desserts commit drops out — it never touched `brats.txt`. (Add `--` before the name, `git log --oneline -- brats.txt`, if Git confuses it with a branch.)


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Writing good commit messages

Your future self reads these. Aim for the middle ground:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
  <th>Message</th>
  <th>Verdict</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td><code>changes</code></td>
  <td><span style="color:red;">Too vague — says nothing</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td><code>Added "Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets" to cheese_curds.txt</code></td>
  <td><span style="color:red;">Too verbose — just repeats the file</span></td>
</tr>
<tr class="hl">
  <td><code>Add cheese curds and desserts</code></td>
  <td><span style="color:forestgreen;">Captures the meaning, briefly</span></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Keep the first line under about [50 characters]{.uwred} and describe the change, not the literal text.

## Where we are

We can now build history on purpose:

- [`git add`]{.uwred} stages changes; [`git commit`]{.uwred} saves them
- [`git status`]{.uwred} shows where things stand
- [`git diff`]{.uwred} shows what changed; [`git log`]{.uwred} shows what we saved
